chunks.text: The coconut palm (Cocos nucifera) is the only living species in the genus Cocos, in the palm family Arecaceae; it was formally described by Linnaeus in 1753. The name comes from 16th-century Portuguese 'coco' ('head' or 'skull'), after the three indentations on the shell that resemble a face; 'nucifera' is Latin for 'nut-bearing'. Genetic studies point to the Central Indo-Pacific — coastal Maritime Southeast Asia and Melanesia (Bismarck Archipelago, Philippines, New Guinea, Solomon Islands) — as its centre of origin and greatest genetic diversity, from where it was carried across the tropics by both ocean currents and, crucially, by Austronesian seafarers who domesticated it during the Neolithic (roughly 3000-1500 BCE). Two broad fruit forms exist: the ancestral 'niu kafa' (thick-husked, angular, adapted for ocean drifting) and the domesticated 'niu vai' (thin-husked, rounder, more endosperm) selected by people for eating. Trees grow up to 30 m tall with a smooth, ringed trunk (old leaf bases shed cleanly), feathery pinnate leaves 4-6 m long, and a fibrous root system of 2,000-4,000 roots rather than a taproot. The tree is monoecious, bearing both male and female flowers in the same inflorescence; about 11 months pass from flower opening to a mature fruit. The fruit is botanically a drupe, not a true nut, with three layers — a glossy outer skin (exocarp), a fibrous husk (mesocarp/coir), and a hard shell (endocarp) enclosing the liquid coconut water and solid white meat (endosperm).

Virtually every part of the coconut palm is used, which is why it is often called the 'tree of life' — in Sanskrit it is kalpa vriksha ('the tree that supplies all needs') and in Malay pokok seribu guna ('tree of a thousand uses'). Culinary uses include fresh or desiccated meat, coconut milk pressed from grated meat (a base for curries and desserts across South and Southeast Asia), coconut water as a drink, fermented coconut water (nata de coco), coconut vinegar, and toddy/arrack fermented from the sap, which can also be boiled down into coconut sugar or jaggery; a single healthy palm can yield around 300 litres of sap a year. Coconut oil, pressed from the dried meat (copra), is a major cooking fat, especially along India's western coast, though its high saturated-fat content (about 33% of the meat by weight, roughly 15% as lauric acid) means health bodies generally advise moderating it in favour of unsaturated fats. Non-food uses are extensive: coir fibre from the husk goes into rope, mats, brushes and mattress stuffing; shells and husks are burned as fuel or made into charcoal or bowls; leaves are woven into thatch, baskets and mats or used to wrap food (like ketupat); and the trunk has historically been hollowed into canoes and drums. In traditional medicine (for example in Cambodia), coconut roots have been used as a mouthwash and folk remedy for diarrhoea, and coconut water is a standard nutrient medium in plant tissue culture. In Hindu ritual across South Asia, coconuts are broken and offered at weddings and temple worship, and coconut-frond fronds (palaspas) are used in Philippine Palm Sunday processions.

Tall coconut varieties begin bearing fruit in 6-10 years and can live 60-100 years, typically producing up to 75 fruits a year though 30 or fewer is more usual; dwarf varieties fruit sooner but live shorter lives. In 2024 global production was about 65.5 million tonnes, with Indonesia, India and the Philippines together supplying roughly 73% of the world's coconuts. Archaeological and genetic evidence shows Pacific coconuts reached Panama in pre-Columbian times via human transport from the Philippines, and later travelled on Manila galleons to Mexico while separate Indo-Atlantic populations were spread by Arab and Portuguese traders to East and West Africa, the Caribbean and Brazil. An unusual harvesting fact: in southern Thailand, pig-tailed macaques have been trained to climb and pick coconuts for an estimated 400 years, a practice now supplemented in places by mechanical climbing aids and even AI-guided harvesting systems.
